subject: chemistry
title: Bonding & Structure: Foundations
welcome_lead: Why does diamond shine while graphite smudges your paper? It's all about structure. Let's see how.
meta_desc: GCSE Chemistry Bonding and Structure foundations — properties of the four main structures plus carbon allotropes.
final_note: You learned the four main structures, their key properties and the family of carbon allotropes.

concepts.def: Lattice of + and − ions held by ionic bonds
Small molecules with weak forces between them
Huge network of atoms joined by covalent bonds
Lattice of metal ions in a sea of free electrons
Different structure of the same element (e.g. carbon)
Hollow carbon cage — sphere or tube of atoms

walkthroughs.body_html:
Almost every solid you meet fits one of four categories.

Giant ionic (e.g. NaCl): high melting point, conducts when molten or dissolved, often soluble in water.

Simple molecular (e.g. CO₂, H₂O): low melting/boiling point, does not conduct.

Giant covalent (e.g. diamond, SiO₂): very high melting point, usually doesn't conduct (graphite is the exception).

Metallic (e.g. iron): high melting point, conducts, shiny, malleable.

To change state, you must overcome the forces between particles.

In simple molecular substances those forces are weak intermolecular forces — easy to break, so low melting points.

In giant ionic, covalent and metallic structures the bonds are strong and there are many of them — so melting points are high.

Conduction needs charged particles that can move: free electrons (metals, graphite) or free ions (molten/dissolved ionic).

Carbon makes several allotropes — same element, different structures:

Diamond: each C bonded to 4 others — giant rigid lattice.

Graphite: sheets of C in hexagons; sheets slide and have free electrons.

Graphene: a single sheet of graphite. Super strong and conductive.

Fullerenes: hollow cages (buckyballs).

Nanotubes: rolled-up graphene cylinders. Strong, conducting, used in electronics.
